From the Seville Conference, the member states adopted an array of commitments and renewed the global financing framework for sustainable development. The Seville commitment is a critical framework which could yield positive results in closing the SDGs financing gap. Our call at this first FFD follow-up forum since SEVIA is simple but urgent. We must maintain momentum and advance the full implementation of the SEVIA commitment by all partners at all levels. We need to translate the commitments that we made by consensus into timely actions that will lead to measurable results. The global community must act together to deliver the existing commitment to mobilize finance at scale for investments across all the goals to move closer to the 2030 targets. In advancing momentum for implementation of the severe commitment, we recognize the efforts that are already taking shape. We welcome the launch of the borrowers platform. which seeks to facilitate peer learning, promote responsible borrowing and lending, and promises to strengthen the voice of borrower countries in the debt architecture. We equally recognize the progress towards promoting disclosure, promoting the discourse and focus on development cooperation effectiveness through the Group of Friends of Development Cooperation Effectiveness launched in January this year. We reiterate the call on an international financial architecture that is fit for purpose, and call for acceleration of reform across the commitment areas agreed upon in Seville. We equally underline the importance of preserving the multilateral trading system, which is driving our economic growth, and we call for implementation of those commitments made in Seville. Zambia remains committed to the implementation of the Seville commitment and continues strengthening efforts to enhance domestic resource mobilization to implement our national and global development agenda. We call on continued support and solidarity anchored on multilateralism as we jointly work towards implementation of our development agenda. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Secretary, the Minister of Finance and National Planning of Zambia. Now I give the floor to Ms. San Adele Okoli, Special Advisor to the President on Finance and the Economy of Nigeria.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Nigeria believes that this forum is coming at a most critical moment for the global economy. The outcome of the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development provided a useful roadmap for addressing the widening financing gap for sustainable development. However, implementation has been slow, and the lived reality for developing countries has not materially improved. Urgency must now define our collective action. Developing countries continue to operate within an international financial architecture that does not adequately reflect their needs, vulnerabilities, or voices. Meaningful reform is overdue. This includes enhanced representation and voting power for developing countries in international financial institutions, as well as equitable access to global financial safety nets, including liquidity support and swap arrangements that remain largely inaccessible to most countries in Africa and the EMD regions. Indeed, access to affordable development finance remains a central constraint. Concessional resources from multilateral development banks are insufficient relative to the needs. compelling countries to rely on commercial borrowing at prohibitively high costs. Mr. President, the growing debt burden across developing countries remains a major impediment to sustainable development. Rising debt service obligations are crowding out critical investments in health, education, infrastructure, and climate resilience. And this is a matter that has been mentioned by many other countries. While we welcome ongoing efforts to strengthen debt transparency and management, including the World Bank's debtor reporting system and capacity building initiatives by IMF and UNCTAD and others, these must be complemented by more effective and timely debt resolution mechanisms, including improved creditor coordination and greater participation of private creditors. We also commend the launch of the Borrowers Platform, which offers a valuable avenue for peer learning and collective engagement among debtor countries. At the national level, Nigeria has undertaken significant reforms to strengthen domestic resource mobilization, anchored within a broader commitment to advancing integrated INFFs as a tool for aligning financing policies with sustainable development priorities. The recent enactment of four major tax reform laws aims to broaden the tax base, streamline compliance, reduce the burden on small businesses and low income

earners, and enhance transparency.

We underscore that the development challenges facing EMEs, particularly in Africa, are not incremental. They're structural and urgent. Addressing them requires bold, coordinated and time bound actions across all pillars of the financing for development agenda, from systemic reforms and debt solutions to scaled up concessional finance and climate aligned investments. I thank you.

I thank the special advisor to the president on finance and the economy of Nigeria. Now I give the floor to Ms. Nancy Ramirez, Director of Cooperation at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala, to be followed by Tanzania

and Uruguay.

Thank you, President, distinguished delegations. Financing for development doesn't just mean discussing figures, it means first of all speaking about people, real opportunities and our capacity to guarantee dignity, equity and sustainable development. Against a global backdrop that is increasingly complex, we note and are pleased to see the organization of the 2026 FFD Forum as a key forum for us to follow up these civil commitments and for us to reaffirm our commitment to robust, inclusive, action-oriented multilateralism. Just a few years before the 2030 deadline, it is clear that the financing gaps continue to exist and are even widening. Many developing countries are facing persistent economic challenges, including entrenched inequality, the persistence of debt and unequal access to concessional financing, even though We account for a major share of the number of people living in poverty. That is why we need to undertake a root and branch reform of the international financial architecture that better reflects the realities and vulnerabilities of our countries. It must also guarantee fair, predictable access to financing for development, looking beyond traditional criteria focusing only on GDP per capita. We reaffirm the importance of strengthening international cooperation for development, including through ODA, with sufficient predictable flows aligned with national priorities. At the same time, we acknowledge the strategic value of mobilizing domestic resources through fairer, more progressive tax systems. We also need to promote responsible private financing to boost sustainable development efforts. There is also an urgent need to address the sustainability of debt from a development approach, incorporating innovative mechanisms that allow us to invest in education, climate resilience and reducing inequalities. We welcome this forum's discussions on debt and the stability of the international system as critical fora that can allow us to come up with structural solutions to these problems. There is also a role for science, technology and digital innovation as key parts of our ability to achieve development as long as it goes hand in hand with national capacity building as well as territorial inclusion. We are committed to the effective implementation of the Seville commitment and to the transformation of this forum into an instrument that can connect global decisions into real impact for people's lives.

I thank the Director of Cooperation at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala. Now I give the floor to Mr. Rishad Baddeh. acting deputy permanent secretary at the Ministry of Finance of the United Republic of Tanzania.

Mr. Chairman, forgive me that opportunity to speak today. The United Republic of Tanzania aligns itself with the statement of the group of 77 China and African group. We meet today at a critical time when global progress toward 2030 agenda is being slowed by fragmentation, geopolitical tension, rising trade barriers, climate change, and climate shocks. Financing the Sustainable Development Report of 2026 makes clear that without urgent action, we risk further falling behind. A financing gap of estimated $4 trillion annually demands coordinated global response. We recall the severe commitment which calls for the scaling up of investment, reforming the international financial system, and strengthening international cooperation. These commitments must now be fully and urgently implemented. Yet the global financial environment is becoming more unequal. Capital flow are increasingly concentrated while least developed countries first reduced access to development finance. Debt challenges limited concessional resources and constraints in financial system reforms are worsening under the current global tension. These pressures are not abstract for Tanzania. The rising global interest rates are increasing increasing borrowing costs and reducing fiscal space. Volatile energy prices are widening and external deficit and fuel inflation. Supply chain disruption are raising transport costs and affects competitiveness. In response, the government remain committed to the resilience and reforms. We are pursuing microeconomic stability, industrialization, agriculture value addition, expanded energy access, and investment in transport and digital infrastructure to support growth and regional integration. We are also asserting fiscal discipline, improving domestic revenue collections, maintaining prudent deficit, enhancing public financial management. These efforts reflect the commitment to stability and long-term development. However, the national efforts alone are not enough. Developing countries need stronger international support, including expanded concessional finance, effective debt restructuring, counter-cyclical lending, fair access to capital markets, and improved allocation of special drawing rights. We therefore call urgent reforms of the global financial architect to ensure it is fair, resilient and capable of delivering on shared commitment. Tanzania remains ready to work with all partners to turn these commitments into real progress towards the sustainable development goal. I thank you.

I thank the acting deputy permanent secretary at the Ministry of Finance of Tanzania. Now I give the floor to Her Excellency Laura Dupuy, Permanent Representative and Chair of G77 and China, speaking on behalf of the group.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. The G77 would like to thank the President of ECOSOC for convening this forum, which provides a valuable space to delve into about what it will take to move the needle between now and 2030 in the pursuit of financing for development. The group believes that the 2026 FFD forum is critical for assessing if and how the Seville commitments are crystallizing into early visible yields. This requires a partnership approach, having in mind the interrelation between the three pillars of the UN Charter. In Seville, the G77 and China joined consensus in reaffirming the financing for development process as the integrative framework for financing sustainable development, including the 2030 agenda. Translating the Seville commitment into a lived reality requires the sustained political will of all actors at all levels across all institutions. Seville will only live up to its potential if those who hold the levels of the international financial architecture, the development partners, the Bretton Woods institutions, the major creditor countries, and the multilateral development banks, MDBs, treat the commitment as a mandate to better frame their work with sustainable development. The momentum from Seville must be captured and implemented urgently. While there has been early yield in implementation following the fourth FFD conference, Member States, the UN system and other actors must continue to join together to advance voluntary commitments alongside the negotiated outcome. Initiatives in the area on debt transparency, concessional finance for developing countries, including for climate action and local currency financing, are welcome. The G77 and China is ready to be a constructive partner in shaping the post-Sevilla landscape. We bring to this forum not a list of complaints, but a determination to work across the lines that too often divide the FFD conversation. Mr. President, the global economic landscape remains fragile and uncertain. The group remains deeply concerned that prolonged geopolitical tensions and conflicts are delivering new shocks to our economies. disrupting global supply chains, undermining national efforts to achieve sustainable development. For the G77 and China, the timely and effective implementation of the Seville commitment is not just an aspiration, but a necessity to close the estimated four trillion US dollar annual financing gap for developing countries. The group notes with alarm the widening disparities in financing capacity. In 2025, official development assistance fell by 23.1% in real terms, the largest annual contraction on record. This trend is unacceptable as it risked reversing hard-won development gains. We urge developed countries to scale up and fulfill their ODA commitments, reaching the target of 0.7% of gross national income for developing countries and 0.15 to 0.2% for the least developed countries. IFIs and multilateral development banks should play a greater role by providing more long-term, affordable, and concessional financing. It is imperative that more support be directed toward developing countries to assist in building sound financial systems, upgrading financial infrastructure, and bolstering crisis resilience, strengthening our collective capacity to finance our sustainable development agendas. Furthermore, the international financial architecture must be reformed to reflect today's realities. We call for more inclusive, representative and effective global economic governance that broadens the voice and representation of developing countries in decision making, including quota and governance reforms within the IMF and the World Bank Group. On debt, developing countries continue to face high borrowing costs and debt servicing burdens that absorb a significant share of public revenues. leaving limited fiscal space to advance sustainable development. Hence, we recall the Seville commitment to promote an intergovernmental process at the United Nations with a view to making recommendations for closing gaps in the debt architecture and exploring options to address debt sustainability, including through holding a dialogue with all relevant stakeholders. Mr. President, international trade remains a critical engine for development, yet it is currently under strain from rising fragmentation, uncertainties, and an increase in trade restrictive measures, which stress the importance of preserving the multilateral trading system as a key driver of economic growth and sustainable development. We reiterate that member states must refrain from applying unilateral economic, financial or trade measures not in accordance with international law that impede or distort the full achievement of economic social development. Additional the group.

I thank the permanent representative of Uruguay and chair of the G73 in China. Now I give the floor to His Excellency Issa Konfrou, permanent representative of Mali, speaking on behalf of the African group. And he will be the last speakers in this session.

Thank you, Mr. President, excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African group. We fully align ourselves with the statement just delivered by Uruguay, on behalf of the Group of 77 and China and wish to highlight the following priority from the perspective of the African group. We meet at a defining moment for global financing for development agenda. The adoption of the CVIA commitment provide a critical opportunity to address systemic gaps in the global financial architecture and to respond to the need of developing countries. In this regard, we welcome the launch of the Borrowers Platform of the 15 April 2026 as mandated under paragraph 48I of the CVR commitment. This is an important step toward its concrete implementation, particularly in strengthening the collective voice and coordination of borrowing countries in the global debt processes. This also require that those actors that hold the levers of the international financial architecture, including international financial institutions, multilateral development banks, and major creditor countries that treat the CVA commitment as a clear mandate to align the policy and operations with sustainable development. for African countries facing high borrowing costs and significant debt servicing burdens, this platform is particularly important. It should enhance transparency, support coordinated engagement, and contribute to advancing the common African position on debt adopted by the African Head of State and Government, which provides unified continental framework to move from debt vulnerability towards sustainable financing, structural transformation and economic sovereignty. Excellencies, the central challenges before us is clear, translating commitment into tangible, timely and scalable results. The global context remain deeply challenging, marked by the tightening financial conditions, rising debt vulnerabilities, declining official development assistance and increasing fragmentation at a time when developing countries face an annual financing gap of $4 trillion. For Africa, these pressures are especially acute and risk reversing hard-won development gains. In this context, the African group highlights three key priorities. First, reforming the international financial architecture. The system must become more inclusive, responsive and representative. This including governance reform in international financial institutions, enhanced participation of developing countries and scaling up access to concessional and affordable long-term finance while addressing systemic bias in risk perception. Second, addressing debt vulnerability in a comprehensive manner. Debt servicing continues to constrain fiscal space across many African countries. We underscore the need for timely, fair and effective debt solutions, improved transparency and inclusive intergovernmental processes with the full participation of all creditors, including private creditors. Third, mobilizing investment and strengthening trade as driver of sustainable development. Current investment flow remain insufficient and uneven. Addressing structural barriers, including the high cost of capital and limited access to risk mitigation is essential. At the same time, trade remain a key engine for Africa's industrialization, including through value addition and regional integration, notably under the African Continental Free Trade Area. Excellencies, we also underscore the importance of advancing international tax cooperation under the United Nations, including ongoing effort toward the UN Framework Convention on international tax cooperation. At the same time, we express deep concern regarding the sharp decline of official development assistance. ODA fell by 23% in 2025, the largest contractions recorded disproportionately affecting African countries and developing countries. I thank you.
